sections.title: Newton's First Law
sections.content: A body remains at rest or in uniform motion in a straight line unless acted upon by a net external force. Inertia is the tendency of a body to resist changes in its state of motion; mass is a measure of inertia.

sections.title: Newton's Second Law
sections.content: The net force on a body equals the rate of change of its linear momentum. For constant mass, acceleration is proportional to net force and inversely proportional to mass.

sections.title: Newton's Third Law
sections.content: For every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. Action and reaction forces act on different bodies, so they do not cancel when considering a single object.

sections.title: Friction
sections.content: Static friction prevents motion up to a maximum value; kinetic friction acts when surfaces slide. The direction of friction opposes relative motion or the tendency of motion.

sections.title: Connected Bodies & Pulleys
sections.content: For systems of blocks and strings, draw free-body diagrams for each mass. Constraints (same string, light pulley) relate accelerations and tensions across the system.
